Start reading here

Read OVK’s historical statement with Sealaska Heritage Institute first, paying attention to its named oral-history evidence and documentary limits. Then explore the culture camp report for a specific account of intergenerational Tlingit learning. This is a local guide to OVK and Kake, not a substitute for broader Tlingit histories. Read source annotations for selected pages, dates, perspective and access limits. This is not a complete history or community endorsement.

  1. U.S. Military to Offer Historic Apology to Kake for Devastating 1869 Bombardment

    Begin with a statement issued by OVK with a Native heritage institute.

  2. Community of Kake Shares Culture Through Distance Learning

    Follow a named OVK coordinator’s account of teaching in 2020.

  3. Kake Cannery National Historic Landmark

    Add labor and preservation history from a documented historic place.

  4. Living in Kake

    Use the city’s orientation narrowly for local coastal context.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

History told with community evidence

The Organized Village of Kake’s 2024 statement with Sealaska Heritage Institute addresses the U.S. military’s 1869 destruction of village sites, canoes and food supplies. It distinguishes Kake oral histories from military records and attributes accounts of the aftermath to Elders Henry Davis and Lincoln Bean. Those attributed recollections belong in the historical record as community testimony. This brief guide neither merges the accounts into a single unattributed narrative nor assigns a casualty total.

Read the sources [1] Organized Village of Kake / Sealaska Heritage Institute

02

Teaching across generations

Sealaska’s September 2020 report follows OVK’s adaptation of Keex’ Kwaan Culture Camp during the pandemic. Coordinator Dylan Lee described the responsibility of passing knowledge to future generations. Younger students received activity packets with Tlingit language exercises; older students joined adapted workshops. This dated example shows cultural transmission as organized work rather than a claim that every citizen participates in the same practices.

Read the sources [2] Sealaska

03

A coastal community and a working history

The City of Kake places the community on Kupreanof Island beside Keku Strait and Frederick Sound and describes its Tlingit history. The National Park Service’s cannery account introduces a related industrial and labor history: buildings, boardwalks and workers’ housing linked salmon processing with a diverse workforce. Its page identifies OVK as the cannery’s manager and describes rehabilitation goals. The municipal and park accounts provide place and preservation context, while OVK remains the named tribal government of this guide.

Read the sources [4] City of Kake [3] National Park Service

U.S. Military to Offer Historic Apology to Kake for Devastating 1869 Bombardment ↗

Publication: 2024-09-16

A community-issued historical statement that explicitly distinguishes Kake oral histories from military records. Named Elders’ testimony is attributed, and the guide avoids reproducing detailed narratives or assigning a casualty total.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Selected body on the attack and aftermath, named oral-history accounts of Henry Davis (1974 interview) and Lincoln Bean (2011 council discussion), discussion of differing historical records, and closing OVK purpose/goals paragraphs. No livestream, image reuse, or full Box of Knowledge book review.

Review recorded: November 2, 2026

Access note: Successful indexed body retrieval on November 2 included the selected historical paragraphs and OVK purpose statement. Two later web-reader attempts timed out; no challenge bypass or retry loop. The already received selected body, not an inaccessible book, supports this record.

Community of Kake Shares Culture Through Distance Learning ↗

Publication: 2020-09-01

A dated report on how OVK adapted Keex’ Kwaan Culture Camp in 2020, with an extended explanation from coordinator Dylan Lee. It supports specific educational activities and intergenerational goals, not present-day program outcomes.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Article body, first occurrence only: camp begun in 1988; 2020 delivery of language-learning/activity packets; adapted workshops for older students; Lee’s explanation of cultural transmission. Repeated page copy, linked harvesting tutorial and photographs excluded.

Review recorded: November 2, 2026

Access note: Public body readable through the web reader; only the stated selected body was reviewed.
